back: The standard shape and size in which a material is supplied before being made into a product — sheets, planks, rods, granules.

front: Why buy materials in standard sizes?
back: They are cheaper and easier to obtain, and parts can be planned to fit with little waste.
A plank is a wide, thick rectangular section; a board is wide and relatively thin.
A long, round section of timber, typically about 6–25 mm in diameter — used for dowel joints, rails and pegs.
Rising in steps of 300 mm, e.g. 1.8 m, 2.1 m, 2.4 m, 2.7 m, 3.0 m.
Sawn: rough with saw marks, close to nominal size, cheaper — hidden structural work. Planed: smooth, a few mm smaller, dearer — furniture and visible work.
Planed all round — timber planed smooth on all four faces.

front: Why check the actual size of planed timber?
back: It is a few millimetres smaller than its nominal size, which affects joints and quantities.

front: Standard sheet size of manufactured boards
back: 2440 × 1220 mm (8 ft × 4 ft), or half sheets of 1220 × 610 mm.
Laying out parts on a standard sheet to waste as little material as possible, allowing for the kerf.
A part made in large quantities to an agreed size, bought ready-made — e.g. screws, hinges, bolts.
Cheaper because they are mass produced, reliable and replaceable, and they save design and making time.
A fixing that lets a product be assembled and taken apart with simple tools — the basis of flat-pack furniture.
A metal dowel in one panel locks into a round cam in the other when the cam is turned.
A cross dowel and bolt — the bolt passes through one part into a barrel nut set across the other.
Flat-packing saves transport space and cost and allows user assembly — but joints are weaker than glued ones and can work loose.
Pellets fed from a hopper into injection moulding, blow moulding and extrusion machines; colour added as masterbatch.
Used for rotational moulding, compression moulding of thermosets, and powder and dip coating of metal.
Sheet, rod, tube, film, 3D printing filament and foam.
